title: The day of miracles
hookLine: Chotrul Duchen, the Tibetan festival at the end of Losar's first fortnight

lines: A BOWL ON A TALL POLE.
cards: In the city of Rajagaha, a sandalwood bowl hangs at the top of a tall pole. A rich merchant has put it there as a test: let any holy man with real powers rise up and take it.

Teachers of other schools come and ask for the bowl, but none of them rises. Then a monk named Pindola lifts into the air, takes the bowl, and comes down to a cheering crowd. It sounds like a triumph.
The Buddha didn't see it that way.

teach.b: In the Vinaya, the Buddha rebukes Pindola: all that, for a wooden bowl, to impress a crowd.
He has the bowl broken up and given to the monks to grind for ointment, and he makes a rule: monks are not to display superhuman powers to lay people.
The tradition then tells a second story, in the commentary on the Dhammapada. Rival teachers hear of the rule and decide the Buddha can no longer perform a wonder, so they challenge him.
The rule binds his disciples, he answers, not himself, the way a king's rule about his orchard binds everyone but the king.
And at Savatthi, tradition says, he performs the twin miracle: fire and water streaming from his body at once.
Tibetan Buddhists remember the Buddha's wonders at Chotrul Duchen, the day of miracles, at the full moon closing the first fortnight of the new year.
Tradition says that on this day the results of what you do, good or harmful, are multiplied many times. So people light butter lamps, give, and make offerings.
In the Kevaddha Sutta, the Buddha names three kinds of wonder: power, reading minds, and instruction. The first two can look like a charm or a trick, he says, and he turns away from them.
The one he praises is instruction, teaching that changes how someone lives.

And a verse in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, points to a quieter kind of wonder: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good."
Beside the festival, that verse gives the multiplying a plain shape: do the good thing a second time.

how: On Chotrul Duchen, Tibetan Buddhists visit temples, light butter lamps, give to monks and to people in need, and make offerings, holding that deeds done on this day are multiplied.

games.q: Pindola has just risen into the air, taken the sandalwood bowl, and come down to a cheering crowd. what does the Buddha do?
o: praises him for silencing the other teachers
rebukes him, has the bowl ground to powder, and makes a rule
asks him to do it again for the king
games.why: he rebukes Pindola for showing off for a wooden bowl, has it ground to powder, and makes a rule against showing powers to lay people.

practice: Bring to mind one kind thing you did recently; small is fine, a message sent, a door held, a meal shared. Enjoy remembering it, the way the verse says, delight in it.
Then picture yourself doing it again, for the same person or someone new.

wordCard.voice: Chotrul Duchen. The day when Tibetan Buddhists remember the Buddha's wonders and, tradition says, every deed counts many times over. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pāṭihāriya: a wonder or marvel; the Kevaddha Sutta names three kinds.

carryVoice: Your line: good deeds multiply. Happiness, the verse says, is the outcome of good. See you tomorrow.
